# Loading data {#sec-loading-data}

::: {.prep-reminder}
{{< var notes-reminder >}} The PREP for this topic: [Lesson 13 PREP: Loading data; numerical derivatives of data]({{< var prep.lesson13 >}}).
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Learning objectives

Throughout this appendix, you will learn to:

- Read data from a `.csv` file using `readtable`.
- Store data files in appropriate locations for use with MATLAB.
- Create MATLAB arrays by extracting data from a MATLAB table.
:::

::: {.motivation}
The most likely use for numerical derivatives (and most of scientific computing) is working with data. Before we can do anything with data, we need to get it into MATLAB.
:::

This appendix is a reference for loading data. It is used in @sec-fd-data and
later chapters.

## CSV files {#sec-csv}

We'll use the [near-Earth asteroid (NEA) discovery dataset](https://cneos.jpl.nasa.gov/stats/totals.html) from NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL). To download it, click **CSV** at the bottom of that page. I saved it as `Asteroid_Data.csv`; you can also [download the copy used in these notes](../files/Asteroid_Data.csv).

**CSV** stands for **comma-separated values**. It is a common format for storing data, and it works with all the usual spreadsheet software (Excel, Google Sheets, etc.). Once you have downloaded the file, try opening it in a spreadsheet:

![`Asteroid_Data.csv` opened in Excel. Your dates will be different, but the structure is the same.](../figures/asteroid_data_excel.png){fig-alt="A spreadsheet with column headers in row 1: Date, NEC, Atira, Aten, Apollo, Amor, PHA-km, PHA, NEA-km, NEA-140m, NEA, and NEO. Each row below is one date, starting with the most recent (12/30/2025, then 12/1/2025, 11/1/2025, and so on, one row per month), with a count in each column." width="60%"}

Each **row** is one date at which data was recorded. Each **column** is one kind of measurement, with a name in the first row. This layout is very common: each date or time of recording creates a new row, with a column for each recorded value.

## Where to save data files {#sec-data-files}

::: {.callout-important}
## Save the data file in the same folder as your `.m` file

MATLAB looks for files in the **current folder**: usually the folder containing the script you are running. Keep each assignment's data file in that assignment's folder (@sec-file-systems), next to the `.m` file that uses it. When working with data, good file system practices are critical: you need to be able to find the file again!
:::

## Loading a CSV file: `readtable` {#sec-readtable}

`readtable` loads a data file into your Workspace:

```matlab
data = readtable("Asteroid_Data.csv");
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## Common problems

**The file can't be found.**

``` {.output}
Unable to find or open 'Asteroid_Data.csv'. Check the path and filename or file permissions.
```

Make sure the data file is in the same folder as your `.m` file, and check the spelling of the file name (including the `.csv`).

**A warning about column headers.** You will see this warning when loading the asteroid data:

``` {.output}
Warning: Column headers from the file were modified to make them valid MATLAB
identifiers before creating variable names for the table. The original column
headers are saved in the VariableDescriptions property.
Set 'VariableNamingRule' to 'preserve' to use the original column headers as
table variable names.
```

Don't worry about that. Some of the column names, like `PHA-km`, aren't valid MATLAB variable names (@sec-variables), so MATLAB renames them, here to `PHA_km`. We'll go with it!
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
`readtable` is a MATLAB command; Octave doesn't have it. The code in the Ed PREPs runs in Octave, so try this part in MATLAB on your own computer.
:::

## Tables {#sec-tables}

The Workspace shows a new type of variable: `data` is a 223×12 **table**. A table is MATLAB's way of storing a dataset. It organizes the data into rows and columns, and each column has a descriptive name. 

``` {.output}
data =

  223×12 table

       Date       NEC    Atira    Aten    Apollo     Amor    PHA_km     PHA    NEA_km    NEA_140m      NEA      NEO
    __________    ___    _____    ____    ______    _____    ______    ____    ______    ________    _____    _____

    2026-10-22    125       41    3513     24408    14888       156    2532       885       11691    42850    42975
    2026-10-01    125       41    3491     24249    14821       156    2532       885       11675    42602    42727
    2026-09-01    124       41    3469     24085    14699       156    2531       885       11644    42294    42418
    2026-08-01    124       41    3455     24005    14639       156    2529       885       11623    42140    42264
    2026-07-01    124       41    3447     23946    14587       156    2527       885       11606    42021    42145

        :           :        :       :         :        :         :       :         :           :        :        :

    1940-01-01     36        0       0         3        6         2       3         8           9        9       45
    1930-01-01     34        0       0         0        5         0       0         5           5        5       39
    1920-01-01     32        0       0         0        3         0       0         3           3        3       35
    1910-01-01     29        0       0         0        1         0       0         1           1        1       30
    1900-01-01     26        0       0         0        1         0       0         1           1        1       27

    Display all 223 rows.
```

- **223×12** means 223 rows and 12 columns.
- **Rows** are horizontal. The first row is `2026-10-22  125  41 ...`: everything recorded on that date.
- **Columns** are vertical. The first column, `Date`, holds the dates. The second column, `NEC`, is the number of near-Earth comets at each date. We may not know what a column name means; we might need to look back at where the data came from. Here, the website says NEC means "near-Earth comets."
- Putting these together: as of 2026-10-22, there were 125 known near-Earth comets.
- The `:` rows mean MATLAB is hiding data to save space. Click **Display all 223 rows** to see everything.

## Extracting columns as arrays {#sec-extract-columns}

Tables are great for storing different types of data side by side (dates next to numbers), but not for doing math. To calculate with a column, extract it as an array: a dot, followed by the column name.

```matlab
nea = data.NEA;         % the number of near-Earth asteroids, as an array
date = data.Date;       % the dates
```

`nea` is an array of numbers, which we can work with like any other array. Each column becomes a column vector (223×1).

`date` is a new type of variable: a **datetime** array. Dates aren't numbers, so we can't use them directly in calculations; see @sec-datetime.


:::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Practice: extract a column

With the asteroid data loaded into `data`, write one line of code that saves the `Atira` column to an array `atira`, without displaying anything.

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
## Answer

```matlab
atira=data.Atira;
```

The column name after the dot must match exactly, including capitalization: `data.atira` gives an error.
:::
::::

## Dates and times {#sec-datetime}

A datetime array stores dates, like `2026-10-22`. To use dates in a calculation, such as dividing by a change in time for a derivative, convert them to numbers first.

`year`, `month`, and `day` pull out each part of a date as a number:

```matlab
y = year(date);         % the year of each date
m = month(date);        % the month of each date
d = day(date);          % the day of each date
```

From these, we can build any time measurement we want. In @sec-ex-nea, the time is **months since January 1, 1900**:
$$t = 12(\text{year} - 1900) + (\text{month} - 1) + \frac{\text{day} - 1}{\text{days in that month}}.$$
`eomday(year, month)` gives the number of days in a month ("end of month day"). The lesson file has this conversion in a function, `convert_datetime_to_number`.
